tagline: Michelin stars, cha chaan tengs, dim sum and a scene that's reinventing itself.
why: Eating out is Hong Kong's favourite pastime, and where you ate last weekend is a guaranteed conversation. The city has everything from Michelin three-star Cantonese to HK$40 cha chaan teng sets, and it's going through big changes as people spend more in Shenzhen and many restaurants close. Knowing the classics, the famous names and the current trends makes you an easy dinner companion.

essentials.title: Cantonese is the backbone
essentials.body: Dim sum, roast meats (char siu, roast goose), seafood, wonton noodles and soups. Freshness and 'wok hei' are the measures of quality.

essentials.title: Cha chaan teng
essentials.body: Hong Kong-style cafés serving milk tea, pineapple buns, macaroni soup and baked pork chop rice: East-meets-West comfort food.

essentials.title: Dai pai dong
essentials.body: Open-air street food stalls, now few and protected; a nostalgic part of the city.

essentials.title: Fine dining and rankings
essentials.body: The Michelin Guide and Asia's 50 Best Restaurants shape reputations. Hong Kong has several three-star restaurants.

essentials.title: Neighbourhoods
essentials.body: Central and SoHo for upscale bars and restaurants, Sheung Wan for trendy spots, Sham Shui Po for cheap eats, Kowloon City for Thai, Wan Chai for everything.

essentials.title: Tough times
essentials.body: Since 2023 many restaurants have closed as locals spend weekends in Shenzhen and tourists spend less. Value and novelty matter more than ever.

now.headline: Restaurant closures
now.detail: Many well-known restaurants closed in 2024-25. Owners blame rent, staffing and northbound spending.

now.headline: Value is king
now.detail: Set menus, deals and casual concepts are winning.

now.headline: Shenzhen is competition
now.detail: Hong Kongers go north for cheaper, trendy food.

now.headline: Bar scene shines
now.detail: Hong Kong bars like Bar Leone keep ranking at the top of Asia's and the World's 50 Best Bars.
